source: A trust splits ownership into management and benefit. Property Code § 111.004(4) defines an express trust as a fiduciary relationship with respect to property which arises as a manifestation by the settlor of an intention to create the relationship and which subjects the person holding title to the property to equitable duties to deal with the property for the benefit of another person. Three roles: the settlor creates the trust and supplies the property; the trustee holds legal title, bound by fiduciary duties; the beneficiary holds the benefit. Section 111.003 trims the field: for the Texas Trust Code, "trust" means an express trust only — not resulting or constructive trusts (court-imposed remedies), not business trusts, and not a deed of trust, despite the name. That last exclusion untangles a Texas vocabulary knot once and for all: the deed of trust of Modules 03 and 08 is a mortgage instrument, not a trust in this sense; only the word is shared.

source: A real estate investment trust (REIT) pools investor capital into a professionally managed portfolio of income properties or mortgages, with interests (shares) that — in the publicly traded form — restore the liquidity that direct ownership lacks: the investor holds real estate exposure in a brokerage account, sellable in a moment.

source: A real estate mortgage investment conduit (REMIC) is the federal vehicle for mortgage securitisation: a pool of mortgages placed in a conduit entity that issues classes of interests to investors, who receive the pooled loans' cash flows. One federal section, read for this course, supplies the defining feature: under 26 U.S.C. § 860A, a REMIC is not itself subject to taxation — the entity level is transparent — and the income of the REMIC is taxable to the holders of interests in it. That single rule is why the structure exists: it lets mortgage pools pass income to investors without an entity-level tax, which made the modern secondary mortgage market's securitisation machinery possible.

source: The note is the debt. A promissory note — Texas practice says real estate lien note when it is secured by realty — is the borrower's unconditional written promise to pay a sum certain, with interest, on stated terms. Its business anatomy is the licence holder's daily vocabulary: the principal; the interest rate (fixed for the term, or adjustable by index plus margin with caps); the term and maturity date; the payment schedule; late charges; the acceleration clause that makes the note's whole balance callable on default (the trigger the deed of trust's machinery waits for); and prepayment terms.

source: A mortgage banker is a lender that does not take deposits. It has no reservoir of customer money. Instead it funds loans out of its own capital plus a short-term revolving line of credit — commonly called a warehouse line in the trade — and then sells the closed loans, usually within weeks, to replenish the line and fund the next batch. The distinction that matters is this: the mortgage banker is the lender. The note is made payable to the mortgage banker, the deed of trust names the mortgage banker, and the mortgage banker's money funds the closing. It then transfers that note to a purchaser.

The note is made payable to the mortgage banker, the deed of trust names the mortgage banker, and the mortgage banker's money funds the closing. It then transfers that note to a purchaser.

source: A mortgage broker is not a lender at all. A broker does not fund. A broker takes the borrower's application, assembles the file, and places it with a lender that will fund it, earning compensation for that intermediary service. Regulation X captures the distinction cleanly in the rule governing the settlement-cost booklet: "If a borrower uses a mortgage broker, the mortgage broker shall distribute the special information booklet and the lender need not do so" (12 C.F.R. § 1024.6(a)(1)). The regulation treats broker and lender as two different persons in the same transaction and assigns the disclosure duty to whichever of them is standing in front of the applicant.

source: A balloon payment is a final payment substantially larger than the periodic payments preceding it, arising because the payment schedule was not designed to retire the debt over the term. A loan amortized on a thirty-year schedule but due in seven years will have twenty-three years of principal left outstanding when the note matures, and that remainder is the balloon. Balloons are not inherently abusive — they are ordinary in commercial lending — but on a home loan they place the borrower in a position of having to refinance or sell on a date fixed years in advance, regardless of what interest rates or property values are doing that month.

source: A contract for deed — in Texas statutory language, an executory contract for conveyance — is a seller-financed sale in which the buyer takes possession and pays the price in installments while the seller retains legal title until the price is paid. Texas regulates these contracts more heavily than almost any other financing device, because historically they were used to sell property to buyers who lost everything on a single missed payment.

source: Comparable. A comparable — a "comp" — is a property similar enough to the subject in location, physical characteristics, use and conditions of sale that its transaction supplies reliable evidence of the subject's value. Three qualifiers do the real work. Similar enough is a matter of degree, and the degree is measured by how much adjustment the comparison requires: a sale needing $40,000 of gross adjustment on a $380,000 house is telling you it is not very comparable. Location in appraisal means the competing market area, which in Texas practice frequently means the same subdivision and even the same school attendance zone, since school boundaries can split a market in half across a single street. Conditions of sale means an arm's-length transaction: a foreclosure sale, a sale between family members, or a relocation-company sale is evidence of something, but not of market value, unless the market in question is itself a distressed market.

source: Multiple listing services. A multiple listing service, or MLS, is a cooperative database through which participating brokerages share listing information and, historically, offers of cooperation and compensation among brokers. In Texas, MLSs are typically operated by or affiliated with local associations, and access is typically conditioned on the participant's membership in the operating organization and on payment of fees. Again: that is how the arrangement commonly works as a matter of private practice. No held source requires a license holder to participate in any MLS, and none dictates the terms on which an MLS operates.

source: A property manager operates real property on behalf of someone else. The owner keeps the title, the equity and the risk; the manager supplies the time, the systems and the judgment. That sentence explains almost everything that follows, including why Texas regulates the work at all: because the manager acts for another person and does so for compensation, the manager stands in the position the Real Estate License Act was written to police. Start with the work, because the law only makes sense once you can see what a manager does in a week. The functions divide into seven streams.

source: The Spanish measure survives. Texas surveying carries its civil-law history in its units: Natural Resources Code § 21.041(3) directs that field notes give the land "by proper field notes with the necessary calls and connections for identification, observing the Spanish measurement by varas." A vara is the old Spanish yard used throughout Texas land records — treated in Texas practice as 33⅓ inches, so that 36 varas equal 100 feet — and old descriptions state distances in varas as a matter of course. A licence holder need not convert units professionally but must recognise them: a call of "950 varas" in an old deed is roughly 2,639 feet, and mistaking varas for feet misplaces a boundary by nearly two-thirds of its length.

The economics are straightforward: pooling buys scale (an apartment complex instead of a condo) and professional management; the investors take fractional interests and rely on the promoter.

source: A deed is the instrument that conveys an interest in real property from grantor to grantee. Its statutory skeleton is short. Property Code § 5.021 — the Texas conveyancing statute you met in Module 06 — requires that a conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold, or an estate for more than one year be in writing, subscribed (signed) by the conveyor or the conveyor's authorised agent, and delivered. Around that core, Texas practice expects: a competent, identifiable grantor whose name matches the record chain; an identifiable grantee; words of grant (Texas needs no magic formula — recall § 5.001's rule that a conveyance passes fee simple unless expressly limited, with no "and his heirs" required); an adequate legal description (Module 04); recital of consideration; and the grantor's acknowledgment before a notary — which, as the recording unit shows, is what qualifies the deed for the public records rather than what makes it valid between the parties.

source: A fraction, a decimal and a percent are three notations for one quantity, and fluent movement among them is most of what real estate math asks of you. To convert a fraction to a decimal, divide the top number by the bottom: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. To convert a decimal to a percent, move the decimal point two places right and add the sign: 0.75 becomes 75%. To convert a percent back to a decimal, move two places left: 5.5% becomes 0.055. Committing a handful of equivalents to memory pays for itself daily — 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%, 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%, 1/3 = 0.3333 ≈ 33.33%, 2/3 = 0.6667 ≈ 66.67%, 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%, and 1/8 = 0.125 = 12.5%.

source: A depository institution is one that takes deposits from the public and lends a portion of those deposits out. Commercial banks, savings institutions, and credit unions are depositories. The defining feature, for our purposes, is that a depository has its own balance sheet of customer deposits available as a funding source. It can originate a loan and fund it with money that is already sitting inside the institution, and if it chooses, it can keep that loan on its own books — hold it "in portfolio" — collect the payments itself, and never involve anyone else. When a depository holds a loan in portfolio it has originated, funded, and serviced the loan, and the borrower deals with one name from application through payoff.

source: A wraparound is a seller-financed transaction in which the seller conveys the property and takes back a note for an amount that includes — wraps around — the balance of an existing loan that remains in place and in the seller's name. The buyer pays the seller on the wrap note; the seller continues paying the underlying lender.

source: A buydown is an arrangement in which a party — most often the seller, sometimes a builder or the borrower — pays money at closing to reduce the borrower's interest rate, either for the loan's full term (a permanent buydown) or for an initial period (a temporary buydown). The funds are typically placed with the lender and applied to make up the difference between what the borrower pays and what the note requires.

source: A stigmatized property is one whose desirability is affected by something that happened in or near it rather than by anything wrong with the bricks and the plumbing: a death in the house, a prior occupant's illness, a crime, a rumour of a haunting. The physical condition is unimpaired; the market reaction is not. Texas addresses part of this territory by statute, and the statute is narrower than its reputation.

source: An encumbrance is any right or interest held by someone other than the owner that burdens the property — diminishing its value or restricting its use — without preventing transfer. The owner can sell; the buyer takes subject to the encumbrance. Encumbrances divide cleanly in two.

source: An adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM, is a loan whose interest rate changes over the term according to a formula rather than remaining fixed. The formula has standard components, which are matters of loan-document drafting and market practice rather than of any statute held for this course: an index, a published rate that moves with market conditions; a margin, a fixed number of percentage points the lender adds to the index; the resulting fully indexed rate; an adjustment period stating how often the rate may change; and caps, which limit how far the rate may move at one adjustment and over the life of the loan. Many ARMs open with an initial rate lower than the fully indexed rate for a stated period.

source: An assumption occurs when a buyer takes over the seller's existing loan, becoming obligated on the note and taking the property subject to the existing lien, instead of obtaining new financing. The attraction is obvious when the existing loan carries an interest rate below the current market: the buyer inherits the seller's rate and avoids the cost of originating a new loan.

source: The zoning commission is the drafting body. Under § 211.007(a) the governing body of a home-rule municipality shall, and of a general-law municipality may, appoint one; it recommends the original district boundaries and the regulations for each district. Section 211.007(b) requires a preliminary report and at least one public hearing before a final report goes to the governing body, which "may not take action on the matter until it receives the final report." Section 211.007(c) requires written notice, before the 10th day before the hearing, to each owner of real property within 200 feet of the property whose classification is proposed to change. Neighbors also have a formal lever: § 211.0061(b) allows a written protest signed by the owners of at least 20 percent of the area covered by the change or of the adjoining area extending 200 feet from it, and under § 211.0061(d) a validly protested change then needs the affirmative vote of at least three-fourths of all members of the governing body.

source: The Commission. The Texas Real Estate Commission is defined in § 1101.002(3) simply as "the Texas Real Estate Commission," and it is built by subchapter B. Section 1101.051(a) provides that it "consists of nine members appointed by the governor with the advice and consent of the senate," comprising "six members who have been engaged in the brokerage business as licensed brokers as their major occupation for the five years preceding appointment" and "three members who represent the public." Members serve staggered six-year terms (§ 1101.055(a)) and are led by a presiding officer whom the governor designates from among the members who are licensed brokers (§ 1101.056(a)). Day-to-day operations belong to an executive director the Commission appoints, together with staff including a general counsel, attorneys and investigators (§ 1101.101), under a policy that "clearly separate[s]" policymaking from management (§ 1101.102).

source: The percent key. The % key is the most misleading key on the keypad because it does different things in different contexts, and often something other than what the user expects. On many calculators 200 × 6 % returns 12 — the key divided by 100 for you. On many of those same calculators, 200 − 6 % returns 188, because the key interpreted 6 as 6 percent of 200 and subtracted 12. On others, the same keystrokes return 194, because the key simply converted 6 to 0.06 and subtracted it. A common error is to assume the key behaves consistently. The safe practice is to never use it: convert the percentage to a decimal yourself by moving the decimal point two places left — 6% becomes 0.06, 5.5% becomes 0.055, 0.5% becomes 0.005 — and multiply. You lose nothing, and you always know what the machine did.

source: A graduated payment plan starts with a payment lower than a fully amortizing payment and increases it on a predetermined schedule — typically each year for a set number of years — until it reaches a level that fully amortizes the remaining balance over the remaining term. The design serves a borrower who expects income to rise. The risk is structural: in the early years the scheduled payment may be less than the interest accruing, and when that happens the shortfall is added to the principal.

source: Index lease and escalation clauses. An index lease adjusts rent periodically by reference to a published index, so rent moves with a measure of general price levels rather than by a flat negotiated step. An escalation clause more broadly is any provision raising rent on a stated trigger — a fixed annual step-up, an index adjustment, or a pass-through of increases in a defined expense. Texas law notices this last variety in one narrow place: Property Code § 92.332(a)(1) provides that a landlord is not liable for retaliation for "increasing rent under an escalation clause in a written lease for utilities, taxes, or insurance." That provision does not authorize escalation clauses — the lease does — but it confirms that such a clause is a legitimate reason for a rent increase and not evidence of retaliation.

source: The termination date requirement is not new in substance, and it has independent teeth. Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(12) has long made it a disciplinary ground to fail "to specify a definite termination date that is not subject to prior notice in a contract, other than a contract to perform property management services, in which the license holder agrees to perform services for which a license is required under this chapter"; Module 10 teaches § 1101.652. Read the qualifier carefully, because it is the part students drop. The date must be definite, and it must be "not subject to prior notice" — meaning an agreement that runs until one side gives thirty days' notice does not satisfy the section. A buyer representation agreement is not a property management contract, so it needs a definite termination date, and now § 1101.563(c)(1)(B) requires the date to be stated in the writing as well.

source: The representation status clause is the hinge between § 1101.563 and § 1101.562. There are two boxes, and they are not both available in every case. If you are representing the buyer, the agreement says you represent the prospective buyer as the buyer's agent. The other box — "does not represent the prospective buyer as the buyer's agent" — is available only "if the only act of real estate brokerage being performed is showing real property under Section 1101.562." That is a narrow gate. You may check the non-representation box only when showing is genuinely the only brokerage act you are performing for that person.

source: An estate is the degree, quantity, nature and extent of a person's interest in land. The primary division is freehold — of indefinite duration, involving ownership — and leasehold — of fixed or determinable duration, involving possession.

source: A life estate is measured by a life. source: An easement is a non-possessory right to use another's land for a stated purpose. It is an interest in land, and it is created and transferred by written instrument or by operation of law.

source: An easement appurtenant benefits a parcel. The benefited parcel is the dominant tenement and the burdened parcel is the servient tenement. This is the easement in most residential transactions — shared driveways, access to a back lot, drainage.

source: An encroachment is an unauthorised physical intrusion — a fence, a roof overhang, a driveway — onto adjoining land. It is discovered by a survey, not by looking. It is both a title problem and a potential dispute, and long-standing encroachments can mature into prescriptive rights. When one is suspected, the professional answer is a survey and, if it exists, legal advice — not a licensee's opinion about where the line is.

source: Expected answer. The water staining is a material adverse fact pertaining to the physical condition of the property, actually known, and must be disclosed in writing under § 54.1-2131 B. The road widening is a matter relating to highways or public streets, which the statute expressly places outside the definition of "physical condition of the property", so the § 54.1-2131 B physical-condition duty does not reach it. That is not permission to mislead: the licensee must still treat the buyer honestly and must not knowingly give false information, and the professional course is to state what is known and direct the buyer to the locality and to VDOT. Toward the seller, who is the client, the road plan is a material fact concerning the property or the transaction of which the licensee has actual knowledge, and § 54.1-2131 A 6 requires it be disclosed to the seller.

source: A trust splits ownership into management and benefit. Property Code § 111.004(4) defines an express trust as a fiduciary relationship with respect to property which arises as a manifestation by the settlor of an intention to create the relationship and which subjects the person holding title to the property to equitable duties to deal with the property for the benefit of another person. Three roles: the settlor creates the trust and supplies the property; the trustee holds legal title, bound by fiduciary duties; the beneficiary holds the benefit. Section 111.003 trims the field: for the Texas Trust Code, "trust" means an express trust only — not resulting or constructive trusts (court-imposed remedies), not business trusts, and not a deed of trust, despite the name. That last exclusion untangles a Texas vocabulary knot once and for all: the deed of trust of Principles I Modules 03 and 08 is a mortgage instrument, not a trust in this sense; only the word is shared.

source: The termination date requirement is not new in substance, and it has independent teeth. Occupations Code § 1101.652(b)(12) has long made it a disciplinary ground to fail "to specify a definite termination date that is not subject to prior notice in a contract, other than a contract to perform property management services, in which the license holder agrees to perform services for which a license is required under this chapter"; Law of Agency Module 10 teaches § 1101.652. Read the qualifier carefully, because it is the part students drop. The date must be definite, and it must be "not subject to prior notice" — meaning an agreement that runs until one side gives thirty days' notice does not satisfy the section. A buyer representation agreement is not a property management contract, so it needs a definite termination date, and now § 1101.563(c)(1)(B) requires the date to be stated in the writing as well.

source: The primary mortgage market is where loans are made. It is the market in which a borrower and an originator meet, an application is taken, and a note and lien are created. Everything in the preceding unit — the depository, the mortgage banker, the broker, the seller, the private lender — is a primary-market actor. The primary market is retail: one borrower, one property, one loan at a time.

source: The secondary mortgage market is where loans that already exist are bought and sold. No borrower participates in it. Its participants are the institutions that originated loans and want to sell them, and the investors who want to own the income stream those loans produce. A loan that is sold in the secondary market does not change: the borrower still owes the same principal at the same rate on the same schedule, secured by the same lien on the same Texas property. What changes is who owns the right to be paid.

source: The affiliated business arrangement exception in § 2607(c)(4) requires three things: a written disclosure to the person being referred of the existence of the arrangement, with a written estimate of the charge or range of charges, delivered at or before the time of the referral (with special timing rules for telephone referrals and lender referrals); that "such person is not required to use any particular provider of settlement services"; and that "the only thing of value that is received from the arrangement, other than the payments permitted under this subsection, is a return on the ownership interest or franchise relationship" (§ 2607(c)(4)(C)). Regulation X implements those conditions in 12 C.F.R. § 1024.15(b)(1)–(3) and requires the disclosure to be "provided on a separate piece of paper."

source: A deed is the instrument that conveys an interest in real property from grantor to grantee. Its statutory skeleton is short. Property Code § 5.021 — the Texas conveyancing statute you met in Principles I Module 06 — requires that a conveyance of an estate of inheritance, a freehold, or an estate for more than one year be in writing, subscribed (signed) by the conveyor or the conveyor's authorised agent, and delivered. Around that core, Texas practice expects: a competent, identifiable grantor whose name matches the record chain; an identifiable grantee; words of grant (Texas needs no magic formula — recall § 5.001's rule that a conveyance passes fee simple unless expressly limited, with no "and his heirs" required); an adequate legal description (Module 04); recital of consideration; and the grantor's acknowledgment before a notary — which, as the recording unit shows, is what qualifies the deed for the public records rather than what makes it valid between the parties.

source: Houston is the well-known example of a very large Texas city that has not adopted conventional use-district zoning; that is common knowledge about how Texas cities have chosen to govern themselves, not a statutory rule, and no source read for this course states it. What the statutes do establish is the structure that makes it possible. Two consequences follow. First, land in the unincorporated portion of a Texas county is not zoned the way land inside a city is, because chapter 211 does not reach it. Second, in a municipality without zoning, recorded private restrictions do far more of the work of separating uses — which is exactly why § 212.151 exists.

source: Reading an estate. Every question about an estate is answered by three smaller questions: How long does it last? What can end it early? Who takes when it ends? Run those three against any granting language — "to A for life, then to B"; "to the church while used for worship"; "to T for five years" — and the estate names fall out mechanically. The licence holder's discipline is humbler and harder: notice when granting language is anything other than a plain fee, and route it to counsel instead of improvising.

source: Doctrine one: protection from forced sale. Property Code § 41.001 exempts a homestead from seizure for the claims of creditors — with a closed list of exceptions, the encumbrances that can be properly fixed on homestead property. The read text names, among them: purchase-money liens (the loan that bought the home); taxes on the property; and work and material liens for improvements, when contracted for in the manner the law requires. The pattern to internalise: the homestead is armoured against general creditors — credit cards, most judgments, business debts — but not against the debts that created or preserved or improved the property itself. A judgment creditor of an ordinary kind cannot force the sale of a Texas homestead; the judgment simply waits, unable to touch the exempt home.

source: The complete list of liens that can bind a homestead. Because "which debts can reach the home" is the whole doctrine, the closed list of § 41.001(b) deserves to be read in full. Encumbrances may be properly fixed on homestead property for: (1) purchase money; (2) taxes on the property; (3) work and material used in constructing improvements, if contracted for in writing as provided by §§ 53.254(a)–(c); (4) an owelty of partition imposed against the entirety of the property by court order or by the parties' written partition agreement — including a debt of one spouse to the other resulting from the award of a family homestead in a divorce; (5) the refinance of a lien against a homestead, including a federal tax lien resulting from the tax debt of both spouses (for a family homestead) or of the owner; (6) an extension of credit meeting the requirements of Article XVI, § 50(a)(6) of the Texas Constitution — the constitutionally regulated home-equity loan; and (7) a reverse mortgage meeting the requirements of § 50(k)–(p) of that article. The structure teaches the policy: every valid homestead lien either created the property interest (purchase money), preserves it against the sovereign (taxes, tax-lien refinance), improved it under written formalities, adjusts ownership itself (owelty), or is a constitutionally supervised borrowing the owner chose. Everything else — however large the debt, however solemn the judgment — stays outside.

source: Finance Code § 343.105 requires a written notice at closing, on a separate document, in at least 14-point type, warning that "[i]ntentionally or knowingly making a materially false or misleading written statement to obtain property or credit, including a mortgage loan, is a violation of Section 32.32, Texas Penal Code," and that the offense is, "depending on the amount of the loan or value of the property," one "punishable by imprisonment for a term of 2 years to 99 years and a fine not to exceed $10,000" (§ 343.105(b)(3)). Read those punishment words for what they are: the Finance Code's prescribed notice language, not the grading provision of the Penal Code. Penal Code § 32.32(b) creates the offense, and § 32.32(c) grades it by "the value of the property or the amount of credit" — a Class C misdemeanor below $100, rising through the misdemeanor and felony grades to "a felony of the first degree if the value of the property or the amount of credit is $300,000 or more." The notice's "2 years to 99 years" describes the top of that ladder, so a license holder should never tell a client that every misstatement on an application carries a 99-year exposure. The same prescribed notice (§ 343.105(b)(3)) includes the applicant's representation "that all statements and representations contained in my/our written home loan application, including statements or representations regarding my/our identity, employment, annual income, and intent to occupy the residential real property secured by the home loan, are true and correct as of the date of loan closing," and § 343.105(c) requires the applicant to verify the information and execute the notice. Section 343.105(d) adds that a lender's failure to give a complying notice "does not affect the validity or enforceability of the home loan by any holder of the loan."
